title: Research
text:
I’m motivated by the shift towards an electrified energy system that makes energy more affordable, secure and clean. Electrochemistry plays an exciting role in this shift, because it sits at the interface between renewable electricity and many of the processes we rely on, allowing more of our energy demand to be electrified, from batteries in electric vehicles to producing chemicals and metals. It also enables renewable electricity to be converted and stored as chemical energy vectors, such as hydrogen or feedstocks made from carbon dioxide. These extend the reach of wind and solar into parts of the economy that can’t yet be electrified directly, like fertiliser production, long-duration energy storage, shipping and aviation.
I have been working in electrochemical research since 2019, with the last five years specifically working on water electrolysis. I am most interested in anion exchange membrane (AEM) water electrolysers: an advanced water electrolysis technology that promises to significantly reduce the cost of green hydrogen production. My PhD focused on developing operando diagnostic techniques to better understand degradation in AEM systems.

title: Research
text:
Research Themes

Electrochemical Testing
Full-cell device testing of performance and durability.

Testing and characterisation of AEM water electrolysers at cell and stack level across multiple EU projects at EPFL - Group of Energy Materials.
Developed in-house testing capability at UCL Electrochemical Innovation Lab and Johnson Matthey. This included commissioning new water electrolyser and carbon dioxide electrolyser test stands and fixtures.



Operando Diagnostics
Identifying the causes of degradation with operando imaging and electrochemical techniques.

Developed an in situ reference electrode technique to separate anode and cathode measurements from the overall cell measurement in AEM and PEM water electrolysers.
Led a team to image membrane thinning in AEM electrolysers using lab-based and synchrotron X-ray microtomography at Diamond Light Source I13-2.
Led a team to study catalyst layer swelling, adhesion and contact in AEM electrolysers at the ESRF ID19.



Method Development
Developing new experimental techniques to address electrochemical research questions.

Developed a three-electrode electrolyser cell, using a COMSOL model to validate reference electrode placement in collaboration with Johnson Matthey.
Designed a miniature electrolyser cell for operando X-ray microtomography in collaboration with Minor Detail.

title: The Case for Operando Techniques
text:
Alkaline water electrolysis using an anion exchange membrane (AEM) has been the focus of a great deal of research in recent years, because of the need to reduce the cost of electrolytic hydrogen1–5. AEM water electrolysis (AEMWE) has distinct advantages over the more established alkaline water electrolysis (AWE) and proton exchange membrane water electrolysis (PEMWE) technologies. If realised, AEMWE would have the low capital cost advantage of AWE, by leveraging inexpensive iron and nickel cell components, while having the flexibility, high current density and high pressure capabilities of PEMWE thanks to a polymer membrane electrolyte. Thus, solving the challenge of durability that AEMWE currently faces is of great interest and importance.
Making AEMWE technology a commercial reality requires the development of electrocatalysts, membranes and porous transport layers, among other cell components. Much of the recent AEMWE literature has focused on new materials like catalysts and membranes. These materials are often characterised ex situ and tested in traditional wet cells, using a rotating ring disc electrode setup for example. While these tests are important for a basic understanding of novel materials, testing with a single cell with a full membrane electrode assembly (MEA) is needed to truly understand how materials will perform under realistic electrolyser conditions.
There are, however, many issues with current single cell testing methods. Certainly, a lack of standardised and reproducible testing is a big challenge acknowledged by the community, and it prevents results reported from different laboratories from being reliably compared1,2,6–9. Progress has been made, with the European Union Joint Research Centre publishing harmonised protocols for testing low temperature water electrolysers in 202110, but uptake of these guidelines has been slow and most laboratories still report their own test protocols. The JRC has since proposed harmonised accelerated stress testing protocols for low temperature water electrolysers11, and inter-laboratory round-robin studies, in which several laboratories test identical materials and hardware using the same protocol, have begun to quantify the scale of the problem. Within Task 30 Electrolysis of the International Energy Agency’s Advanced Fuel Cells Technology Collaboration Programme, round robins have established reference hardware and protocols for PEMWE12,13 and liquid alkaline electrolysis14. AEMWE has lagged behind, and the first multi-laboratory single cell AEMWE round robin found that both in-house and cross-lab variation were even greater than for PEMWE, with cross-lab differences of up to 476 mV at 1 A cm-2 in pure water, compared with a maximum of 27 mV in the first PEMWE round robin12,15. Many studies that investigate new catalysts and membranes do publish MEA testing procedures and data, but the complexity of single cell electrolyser tests means experimental design varies significantly between research groups. Aside from the obvious differences of catalyst, ionomer and membrane, different porous transport layers, feed solutions and MEA fabrication techniques may be used, along with a multitude of other variables. Furthermore, many papers neglect to publish the full detail of their testing, making their work challenging to reproduce16. As a result, comparing the performance of novel catalysts and membranes from different studies is challenging.
If the benefit of single cell testing is the ability to see how new materials and components will perform and degrade in a real electrolyser, the drawback is the limited information that can be acquired during the test. Most single cell tests are limited to two-electrode electrochemical characterisation, including polarisation curves, impedance spectroscopy and cyclic voltammetry. These techniques are powerful, but they probe the cell as a whole, so distinguishing between processes related to each cell component can be challenging. This means that extensive testing of different MEAs is required, changing only one variable at a time, to narrow down the exact cause of performance differences. Post-mortem analyses of the cell components, like electron microscopy and X-ray spectroscopic techniques, help reveal the physical and chemical changes to the cell but necessitate its disassembly, which means the information obtained is less relevant to the materials within a real operating electrolyser.
Single cell testing can, however, be enhanced by additional electrochemical measurement devices such as reference electrodes, as well as by complementary in situ and operando imaging and spectroscopic techniques in specially designed test fixtures. By correlating different complementary measurements made during each electrolyser test, it is possible to achieve a richer and more detailed understanding of the processes occurring during electrolyser operation. Such an understanding is necessary for the advancement of electrolyser technology.
In my PhD, I used two different techniques to enhance single cell measurements: in situ reference electrodes and operando X-ray microtomography. By using an in situ reference electrode, the anode and cathode of the same MEA could be studied simultaneously in a three-electrode measurement that deconvolutes the half-cell potentials from the overall cell potential17. Operando X-ray microtomography, meanwhile, enabled the physical changes to the internal structure of the electrolyser cell to be observed and correlated with changes in electrochemical performance18.

title: Looking Inside the Electrolyser: The Case for Operando Techniques
section: From the lab bench to the real cell
text:
From the lab bench to the real cell
Commercialising AEMWE means developing better electrocatalysts, membranes, porous transport layers and other cell components. Much of the recent literature focuses on new materials, which are often characterised ex situ and tested in conventional wet cells, such as a rotating ring disc electrode setup. These tests are valuable for fundamental understanding, but to know how a material will actually behave in an electrolyser, it has to be tested in a single cell with a full membrane electrode assembly (MEA).

title: Looking Inside the Electrolyser: The Case for Operando Techniques
section: The problem with single cell testing
text:
The problem with single cell testing
Single cell testing comes with its own challenges. A lack of standardised, reproducible testing is widely acknowledged as a major obstacle, making it hard to compare results between laboratories (Du et al. 2022; Miller et al. 2020; Xu et al. 2022; Lee et al. 2022; Henkensmeier et al. 2021; Titheridge and Marshall 2024).

Du, Naiying, Claudie Roy, Retha Peach, Matthew Turnbull, Simon Thiele, and Christina Bock. 2022. “Anion-Exchange Membrane Water Electrolyzers.” Chemical Reviews 122 (13): 11830–95. https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.chemrev.1c00854.

Miller, Hamish Andrew, Karel Bouzek, Jaromir Hnat, et al. 2020. “Green hydrogen from anion exchange membrane water electrolysis: a review of recent developments in critical materials and operating conditions.” Sustainable Energy & Fuels 4 (5): 2114–33. https://doi.org/10.1039/C9SE01240K.

Xu, Qiucheng, Liyue Zhang, Jiahao Zhang, et al. 2022. “Anion Exchange Membrane Water Electrolyzer: Electrode Design, Lab-Scaled Testing System and Performance Evaluation.” EnergyChem 4 (5): 100087. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.enchem.2022.100087.

Lee, Sol A, Jaehyun Kim, Ki Chang Kwon, Sun Hwa Park, and Ho Won Jang. 2022. “Anion exchange membrane water electrolysis for sustainable large‐scale hydrogen production.” Carbon Neutralization 1 (1): 26–48. https://doi.org/10.1002/cnl2.9.

Henkensmeier, Dirk, Malikah Najibah, Corinna Harms, Jan Žitka, Jaromír Hnát, and Karel Bouzek. 2021. “Overview: State-of-the Art Commercial Membranes for Anion Exchange Membrane Water Electrolysis.” Journal of Electrochemical Energy Conversion and Storage 18 (2): 024001. https://doi.org/10.1115/1.4047963.

Titheridge, Laura J., and Aaron T. Marshall. 2024. “The Rationale for a Standardized Testing Protocol for Anion Exchange Membrane Water Electrolyzers.” ACS Energy Letters 9 (3): 1288–94. https://doi.org/10.1021/acsenergylett.4c00239.

Tsotridis, Georgios, and Alberto Pilenga. 2021. EU harmonised protocols for testing of low temperature water electrolysers. Publications Office of the European Union.

Smith, Graham, and Edmund J. F. Dickinson. 2022. “Error, reproducibility and uncertainty in experiments for electrochemical energy technologies.” Nature Communications 13 (1): 6832. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-34594-x.
There has been progress. In 2021 the European Union Joint Research Centre published harmonised protocols for testing low temperature water electrolysers (Tsotridis and Pilenga 2021). Uptake has been slow, however, and most groups still use their own procedures. Beyond the obvious variables of catalyst, ionomer and membrane, groups differ in their porous transport layers, feed solutions, MEA fabrication methods and much more. Many papers also omit important experimental details, making the work hard to reproduce (Smith and Dickinson 2022). The result: comparing new catalysts and membranes across studies is difficult.

title: Looking Inside the Electrolyser: The Case for Operando Techniques
section: Limited information from a whole-cell view
text:
Limited information from a whole-cell view
Even a well-designed single cell test has a fundamental limitation: it yields relatively little information. Most tests rely on two-electrode electrochemical methods such as polarisation curves, impedance spectroscopy and cyclic voltammetry. These are powerful, but they probe the cell as a whole, making it hard to attribute changes to a specific component. Pinning down the cause of a performance difference therefore often requires testing many MEAs, changing one variable at a time.
Post-mortem analysis, such as electron microscopy and X-ray spectroscopy, can reveal physical and chemical changes to the components. But it requires taking the cell apart, so what you see is no longer quite what was happening inside the operating electrolyser.

title: Looking Inside the Electrolyser: The Case for Operando Techniques
section: Seeing more while the cell runs
text:
Seeing more while the cell runs
Single cell testing can be greatly enhanced with additional measurement tools, such as reference electrodes, and with in situ and operando imaging and spectroscopy in purpose-built test fixtures. Correlating these complementary measurements during a single test builds a much richer picture of what happens during electrolyser operation, and that understanding is essential for advancing the technology.
My PhD research used two such techniques:

In situ reference electrodes. By adding a reference electrode, the anode and cathode of the same MEA can be studied simultaneously in a three-electrode measurement, separating the individual half-cell potentials from the overall cell voltage, \(E_{\text{cell}}\).
Operando X-ray microtomography. This allows the internal structure of a working electrolyser to be imaged, so physical changes can be observed directly and correlated with changes in electrochemical performance.

Together, these approaches help move us from asking whether an electrolyser degrades to understanding where and why.
